p: The word Renaissance is French, and means rebirth. It was made popular as the name of a period of history only within my own lifetime, by the French historian Jules Michelet in eighteen fifty-five, and still more by a Swiss professor, Jacob Burckhardt of Basel, whose book The Civilisation of the Renaissance in Italy appeared in eighteen sixty and will, I am told, shortly be put into English. Burckhardt argued that in Italy in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, modern man was born: that the Italians of that age first regarded themselves as individuals, rather than as members of a class, a guild or a church; and that they found the model for this new kind of life in the rediscovered literature and art of ancient Greece and Rome. It is a dazzling argument and, like most dazzling arguments, it is too simple. But it describes something that really happened.

Italy in the fourteenth century was not a nation but a patchwork of small states: the kingdom of Naples in the south, the lands of the pope in the middle, and in the north a crowd of rich and quarrelsome cities, Florence, Venice, Milan, Genoa and many more. They were rich from trade and banking and the manufacture of cloth, and they were full of merchants and lawyers who could read, who had money to spend, and who wanted to know how to live and to govern a city. The ancient Romans, whose ruins lay all about them, seemed to offer the answer. The Romans had been citizens of a republic. They had written about duty, friendship, glory, eloquence and the active life. They had built magnificently.

The scholars who devoted themselves to recovering ancient literature were called humanists, because they studied what were called the humanities, the studies proper to a man: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy. The first and most famous was Francesco Petrarca, whom we call Petrarch, a poet of the fourteenth century, who hunted for lost manuscripts of Cicero in monastery libraries and was the first to describe the centuries since the fall of Rome as an age of darkness. His successors ransacked the libraries of Europe; Poggio Bracciolini found in a German monastery, in fourteen seventeen, a copy of the poem On the Nature of Things by the Roman poet Lucretius, which explains the world as the chance movement of atoms and denies that the gods care for mankind. It had been all but lost for a thousand years. After the fall of Constantinople, Greek scholars fleeing to Italy brought Greek manuscripts and the knowledge to read them, and Plato, almost unknown in the West for centuries, was translated into Latin at Florence by Marsilio Ficino.

The humanists also invented, or revived, a critical method that is the foundation of my own profession. Lorenzo Valla, in fourteen forty, proved by an analysis of its language that the so-called Donation of Constantine, a document in which the emperor Constantine was supposed to have given the pope dominion over the western empire, and upon which the papacy had rested claims for centuries, was a forgery written hundreds of years after Constantine's death. He showed that its Latin was not the Latin of the fourth century. It was a revolution in method: a text was to be judged not by its authority but by evidence.

It is chiefly through its art that the Renaissance is remembered. In Florence, early in the fifteenth century, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi raised the great dome of the cathedral, the largest since antiquity, by methods of his own devising, and worked out the mathematical rules of perspective, by which a painter can represent depth upon a flat surface as the eye sees it. Masaccio painted figures with weight and shadow, standing in real space. Donatello made the first free-standing nude statue since ancient times. Then came the generation of Leonardo da Vinci, painter, engineer and anatomist, who filled his notebooks with designs for flying machines and studies of the human body and left, it seems, more works unfinished than finished; of Michelangelo, who carved the David and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, standing on a scaffold for four years with his head bent back, so that, as he complained in a comic poem, his beard pointed at heaven and the paint dripped onto his face; and of Raphael, whose serenity seemed to his contemporaries the perfection of art.

This flowering depended on money. The Medici family, bankers to the pope and the princes of Europe, ruled Florence in all but name for most of the fifteenth century, and spent lavishly on art and learning, partly from love of beauty, partly for the glory of their family, and partly, I suspect, to make their money seem respectable. Cosimo de' Medici is said to have feared for his soul on account of his usury and to have built churches by way of insurance.

The Renaissance was not only an age of beauty. It was an age of incessant war between the Italian states, fought by hired captains, until in fourteen ninety-four the French invaded, and Italy became for sixty years the battlefield of France and Spain. It was the age of the Borgia pope Alexander the Sixth and his son Cesare, of poisonings and assassinations, and of Niccolò Machiavelli, a Florentine official who, in a little book called The Prince, written in fifteen thirteen, advised rulers that it is safer to be feared than loved, and that a prince must learn how not to be good. His name has become a byword for cunning. He was, in fact, a patriot and a republican, who described politics as he saw it practised. That is a habit that has never made a man popular.

The Renaissance spread from Italy across Europe in the sixteenth century, to the France of Francis the First, to the Netherlands of Erasmus, and to the England of Sir Thomas More, whose Utopia, a word he made from Greek and which means no place, imagined an ideal commonwealth, and at last to the England of Shakespeare. It bequeathed to us a confidence in human powers, a reverence for the classics that governed the education of every English gentleman until my own day, and a way of looking at the world, critical, curious and individual, that we call modern. Burckhardt overstated his case. But he was not wrong that something was born.
